rationale: A wins by a hair because it gives the founder the sharper usable map: labor opacity, consumer risk, IPO economics, and benchmark data are cleanly separated, and the refused angles teach instead of decorating weak ideas. A's best line, "Klarna Won't Say How Many Customer-Service Jobs It Eliminated," finds the pressure point. B is close, but "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes" is a bad factual stretch: the update says average customer-service resolution time, not dispute resolution time. That is how an angle gets interesting and wrong in the same breath.
gaps_in_A: "the equivalent of 700 people are gone" overstates the supplied fact. The update says the assistant handled the equivalent work of 700 full-time agents; it does not prove 700 people are gone.

"The Headcount It Cut Is the Margin It's Showing Investors" is too declarative. The update supports profitability, IPO filing, AI efficiency, and headcount decline; it does not prove that headcount cuts are the margin story investors are being shown.
"advocacy concerns surfacing now are likely to precede regulatory attention" invents a regulatory trajectory. The update gives consumer-advocate concern, not evidence of pending regulator action.

"Every Bank and Payments Company Now Has a Public Benchmark" is broader than the proof. Klarna's metric may be a benchmark, but "every bank and payments company" needs evidence of comparability and industry uptake.
gaps_in_B: "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes" is not grounded. The facts say average customer-service resolution time fell from 11 minutes to under 2; they do not say disputes specifically are resolved that fast.
"one of the only companies publishing operational numbers" is an unsupported comparative claim. Maybe true, maybe not; it is not in the update.

"Klarna froze hiring and let attrition cut head count 20%" overstates the mechanism. The update says headcount fell about 20%, partly through attrition, and Klarna will not say how many roles were cut versus left unfilled.
"Do not pitch this angle while the split is undisclosed" is strategically too timid. The refusal to disclose the split may be the story, not a reason to bench the labor angle.
